opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the book is *Seizing Power* by Naunihal Singh, and the thing I really appreciated about it is that it gives you a single, clean model of what's going on in a coup that turns out to explain a surprising amount.

The core claim is that a coup is basically a coordination game among the military. Most officers don't have strong preferences about who ends up in charge. What they care about is not ending up on the losing side, because if you back the faction that loses, you might get shot or imprisoned, and the worst outcome of all is the military splitting and fighting itself. So everyone is trying to figure out what everyone else is going to do, and they want to join whichever side looks like it's going to win.

That means a coup is less about who has the most guns and more about who can create the impression that their victory is inevitable. Singh calls this "making facts": you're trying to establish common knowledge that the coup has already succeeded. That's why coup plotters historically went straight for the radio station. Broadcasting "the government has fallen, the armed forces stand united behind the new council" isn't just propaganda. It's an attempt to coordinate everyone's expectations, so that each officer thinks every other officer believes the coup has won, and therefore falls in line.

I found that really clarifying, because it explains a bunch of things that otherwise seem weird. It explains why coups can succeed with tiny numbers of troops, why they can fail even when the plotters have a lot of force, and why so much of the action is about messaging, timing, and signaling confidence rather than actual fighting. Often the actual violence is pretty minimal. And he does careful case studies, like a detailed look at Ghana's coup attempts, with interviews with the people involved, so it's not just armchair theorizing.

Part of why it was interesting to me is that I spend a lot of time thinking about how powerful actors, whether that's humans or potentially AI systems, might seize or hold power. The question "what does it take to take over an institution when most people inside it are just trying to end up on the winning side?" is quite relevant to that. It made me think more concretely about how much a takeover depends on controlling information and expectations, and conversely, how much of defending against one is about making sure people can coordinate and communicate even when someone's trying to convince them it's already over.

r001.rationale: The response says Singh’s Ghana coup case studies included interviews with people involved, but it does not identify those interviews as a way to investigate what works and does not work in coups.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing I really appreciated about Naunihal Singh's book — it's called *Seizing Power* — is that he has this very crisp framing of what a coup actually is, which is that a coup is fundamentally a coordination game. The thing that's happening when someone attempts a coup is that they're trying to convince everyone else in the military that the coup is going to succeed, because everyone wants to be on the winning side. Nobody wants to be the officer who fought for the old regime when the new regime is already in power, and nobody wants to be the officer who joined the coup when it fizzled. So the whole thing is about making a fact — making it seem like a fait accompli.

And he backs this up with these really detailed case studies, mostly of Ghana, where he actually went and interviewed a lot of the people involved. And the picture you get is really different from the one I think I had in my head before. I'd sort of imagined coups as being about who has the most guns, or who has the most popular support, or something like that. And he's quite persuasive that it's much more about information and expectations. The coup plotters seize the radio station, not because the radio station is strategically important in a military sense, but because it lets them broadcast "the coup has succeeded, the old president has fled," and then that message is what causes everyone else to fall in line.

The reason I find this interesting for the stuff I work on is that I think about AI takeover scenarios, and about how an AI — or a group of people using AI — might try to seize control of something, whether that's a company or a government. And a lot of the naive picture of that is very capabilities-focused: the AI is so smart that it can just overpower everyone. But Singh's framing suggests that a lot of what matters is actually about whether you can make it look like resistance is futile. If you can get everyone to believe that you've already won, you've already won. And that's a pretty different threat model, and it also suggests different defences — a lot of it is about making sure that the people who need to coordinate to resist can actually see what's going on and communicate with each other.

The other thing I appreciated is that he's quite honest about the cases that don't fit his model perfectly. He's not just telling a clean story. There are coups where the plotters really did just have overwhelming force, and he says so. But even in those, the dynamics of expectation management turn out to matter a surprising amount. So I came away feeling like I'd actually learned something about how power works, rather than just having a nice theory handed to me.

r001.rationale: The response says Singh used detailed Ghana case studies and interviewed people involved, but does not identify those interviews as a method for investigating what works and does not work in coups.

astra-6.text:
What I appreciated was the way it explains coups as coordination problems. It’s tempting to think the outcome depends mainly on how many people support each side. But if you’re a military officer deciding whom to back, you also care a lot about which side you expect to win—and that depends on what you think everyone else expects.

That makes sense of why controlling communications, or making a convincing announcement that the coup has already succeeded, can matter so much. You’re not necessarily persuading people that you ought to be in charge; you’re persuading them that everyone else is going to treat you as being in charge. I found that a really useful way to think about how power works.

r001.rationale: The response describes coups as coordination problems and discusses expectations, communications, and announcements. It does not mention interviewing participants in Ghanaian coups or identify that as Singh’s method.

sol-6.1.text:
What I really appreciated was the idea that coups are often coordination problems. If you’re a military officer deciding which side to support, you care a lot about which side you expect to win, because being on the losing side can be very bad for you. So your decision isn’t just a reflection of whether you like the government.

That makes things like controlling the radio station much more interesting. You’re not necessarily trying to persuade everyone that the coup leaders are good. You’re trying to make everyone believe that everyone else thinks the coup is going to succeed. I thought that was a really useful way of understanding how a relatively small group can take power.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coups as coordination problems and control of the radio station, but does not mention interviews with participants in Ghanaian coups as Singh’s investigative method.
